cards.title: Specific Headlines Over Clever Headlines for Paid Ads
cards.summary: Write ad headlines that state the offer and audience plainly rather than chasing cleverness, because clicks for the wrong reason convert to sales far less often.
cards.use_when: Writing or reviewing headlines for paid social, search, or display ads and deciding between a clever hook and a specific offer-based headline.
steps: Before finalizing, ask what the reader thinks you are selling after reading only the headline. If they cannot tell, rewrite.
Build the headline from the core elements: product/promise, key benefit, time-to-deliver or other qualifier, price or savings signal, and credibility (expert, years, results).

Check the headline against the audience it should attract. A clever hook like 'Sticky Web' may get clicks but from people who don't need the service; a specific headline attracts only qualified buyers.
Reserve cleverness for tests only, with a budget you're willing to risk; judge by qualified clicks and purchase conversion, not raw CTR.
Add psychological triggers via the source's 22 headline starters rather than puns, and put one clear benefit in the headline.
caveats: The source's position that 'clever' headlines lose 60% of scrollers is a heuristic, not verified by the source's own testing data.
Averages can mask brand-recall or entertainment-first campaigns where cleverness aids shareability, though the author disputes that framing.

cards.title: Run Multiple Ad Formations in One Placement for 1+1=3
cards.summary: Place more than one ad in the same issue or channel so repeated exposure compounds response, using proven right-page and spread formations.
cards.use_when: Planning ad frequency and placement for print inserts, catalog pages, or multi-ad buys where a single placement isn't generating traction.
steps: Accept that any individual insertion is read by only a percentage of your audience; frequency compensates for partial attention, so don't evaluate a single ad on one run.

Choose a multi-ad formation ranked by the source's tested effectiveness: three single-page ads in sequence on the right; two single-page ads on right pages across different sections; double-page spread; single right-page ads; single left-page with strip ad on the right; left-page ads; right-page checkerboard (quarter-page ads in four corners); left-page checkerboard; half-page upper right; half-page lower right.
Keep the ad creative distinct enough that each exposure adds new information (different benefits, proof, or angles) rather than repeating verbatim in the same issue.
For ecommerce, translate to sequential creative in one placement (carousel, multi-slot Story, or repeated ad set across audience segments) with each panel a different selling angle.
Test single-ad versus multi-ad executions because the source's multi-page gains are described as an aggregate, not guaranteed.
caveats: Starch's 1+1=3 result is a citation from decades-old print research; the exact multiple is not guaranteed to transfer to digital placements.
Multi-ad buys raise cost, so compare response lift against incremental spend per placement.

cards.title: Offer Longer Guarantees to Increase Confidence and Reduce Returns
cards.summary: A strong, longer-than-competitor guarantee lowers pre-purchase stress, boosts conversion, and paradoxically lowers returns by removing the beat-the-clock mindset.
cards.use_when: Setting return, refund, or satisfaction policy on a product page, in ads, or in checkout, especially for high-ticket or unfamiliar products.
steps: Pick a guarantee length longer and stronger than your industry norm. The source offers a one-year money-back guarantee on many products; longer options include six months, one year, five years, ten years, or lifetime.

Explain the rationale on the page: short guarantees (30/60/90 days) keep buyers watching the deadline and condition them to return in time; long guarantees build confidence in the product and reduce returns.
Present the guarantee prominently with visual weight—certificate border, signature under it—on the PDP, in ads, in brochures, and on the site rather than burying it in policy fine print.
Use the guarantee as a competitive wedge when rivals have weak or absent guarantees, asking in bold: 'Why do our competitors guarantee their [product] for only 90 days?'
Consider higher-risk versions like double-your-money-back where credits offset buyer skepticism, but only where you can absorb the cost.
caveats: The Hormel double-money-back example (only 12 women took advantage) is a historical case study, not a prediction of your return rate.
The claim that longer guarantees create fewer returns is sourced to studies but not specified; test for your category and price point.

cards.title: Use Square-Root Rule to Decide Ad Size vs. Color
cards.summary: Attention grows roughly with the square root of ad area, so quadrupling size roughly doubles attention while color can be the cheaper attention lever.
cards.use_when: Budgeting between buying more ad space versus adding color or improving the ad's creative, for any paid placement where you can increase either size or color.
steps: Apply the rule of thumb: doubling attention requires enlarging ad area by 400% (e.g., quarter-page to full-page); tripling requires 900%, which is only practical for very small classified ads or by going multipage.
Check cost trade-offs: if adding color costs less than enlarging the ad, opt for color. Starch research indicates color affects readership more than size does.

Use specific color findings: color-supported reading is 60% higher than black-and-white and 40% higher than two-color ads; the readership gap between B&W and four-color is larger than between one- and two-page color.
Reserve B&W for ads emphasizing end benefits, dramatic situations, or intellectual appeals per Starch guidance, and color for competitive, benefit-dense visual pitches.

Reject the naive assumption that 4x size yields 4x response; correct internal or client expectations with the research table (e.g., Strong: half-page 141%, full-page 215%; Starch: half-page 168%, full-page 314%).
caveats: The individual studies (Scott, Strong, Hotchkiss, Starch, Adams) disagree widely; the square-root rule is a derived rule of thumb, not a precise formula.
All cited data is from print-era research; treat digital equivalents as directional, not benchmarked.

cards.title: Stop Worrying About Page Position, Except the Fantastic Four
cards.summary: Inside-page position (left/right, front/middle/back) barely affects ad effectiveness; only cover and specific high-attention slots justify premium placement.
cards.use_when: Negotiating premium placement rates for inserts, magazine ads, newsletters, or newsletters-like digital placements where you're deciding whether to pay extra for position.
steps: Skip paying a premium for generic front, middle, or back inside placement; studies by Starch, Stanton, Nixon, National Magazine, Lucas and others found negligible difference—what matters is the offer and execution.

If paying for premium placement, target the Fantastic Four, based on Starch INRA Hooper's comparison of 618 cover ads vs. 10,789 inside single-page four-color ads: inside front cover (+29% 'Noted' score), opposite table of contents (+25%), back cover (+22%), inside back cover (+6%).

Apply to digital analogies: pay extra only for high-visibility positions that behave like cover slots (top-of-feed placements, above-the-fold takeovers, above-the-fold PDP hero) rather than any premium slot.
Redirect budget saved on positioning into offer strength and copy/design, since the research points there for effectiveness.
Test any premium placement against a standard placement to confirm the lift pays for the rate differential.
caveats: Fantastic Four percentages come from print magazine testing; treat as directional for digital placements and verify with your own tests.
Cover-slot premiums may be more about brand prestige than measured DR lift in your channel.

cards.title: Choose Colors and Paper/Ink Combos by Measured Readership
cards.summary: Consumer color preference ranks blue, red, green, violet, orange, yellow; certain paper/ink and color pairings measurably improve or wreck readability.
cards.use_when: Specifying packaging colors, PDP/landing-page palette, ad backgrounds, and print insert paper/ink for maximum readership and shelf impact.
steps: Lead with blue (1st) and red (2nd) for prominent design elements to match the tested worldwide preference ranking; green, violet, orange, then yellow follow.

Adjust for audience age: red is first among infants, then preference shifts; as people age, blue rises while yellow declines (blue light absorption in aging eyes is cited as one theory). Yellow is riskiest for older audiences.
Account for small gender differences: men rank orange 5th/yellow 6th; women swap yellow 5th/orange 6th.

For readable print: white and yellow are best paper colors; use black, dark blue, and red inks for maximum impact. The best combo is black ink on yellow paper; the worst is red ink on green paper (near-unreadable, fully unreadable to colorblind readers).
Avoid confusion with category-owned colors: Canada Dry's sugar-free ginger ale shifted from red (read as 'cola') to green/white, and sales rose more than 25 percent—an example, not a promise.
Remember the apparent-weight illusion: darker colors make packaging or products feel heavier, lighter colors feel lighter.
caveats: Canada Dry's 25%+ result is a single case study, not a benchmark.
Color preference research is older; brand identity and audience segmentation may override raw preference rankings.

cards.title: Use Psychological Pricing: Fractional for Value, Round for Prestige
cards.summary: Odd/fractional price endings signal value while rounded whole numbers signal premium quality; the specific endings matter (99 > 95, 88 and 79 and 98 also signal value).
cards.use_when: Setting prices on product pages, bundles, cart upsells, and ad copy for mass-market versus premium tiers.
steps: For value-positioned products, use fractional endings that research supports: 99 (confirmed stronger than 95), plus 79, 88, and 98. Avoid endings in 49, 50, 90, or 00 for value perception.
For prestige-positioned products, use rounded whole numbers only (e.g., $1,000.00 rather than $999.95), matching retailer practice at Nordstrom and SaksFifthAvenue.com.
Use the sale-perception effect: prices ending 98 or 99 are more likely read as on-sale and as not-recently-raised by consumers, useful in promo copy.
Consider context: mass retail heavily uses psychological pricing (Wal-Mart's preference for '97'), so it's a default for D2C value brands and friction-laden high-ticket categories.
Pair price-ending strategy with value-conveying copy (amortization, comparison to coffee-a-day, worth-vs-cost framing) rather than relying on the number alone.
caveats: Specific study results: 99 catalog produced 8% greater sales than 00 and 88 matched 00 (Schindler & Kibarian 1996); treat as example lift, not a universal benchmark.
Rutgers (2000) found a $49.99 dress judged lower quality than a $50 one—relevant caution for premium claims.
Ending effects can diminish in subscription or B2B contexts; test in your category.

cards.title: White-Wrap Your Ad to Boost Attention Without More Copy
cards.summary: Buying more space and surrounding the original ad with white space increases attention more efficiently than filling the extra space with copy.
cards.use_when: Designing a PDP hero, landing-page module, or print ad where you can buy more space and are deciding between more content and more whitespace.
steps: Buy more space (e.g., go from quarter-page to half-page) but keep the original ad intact in the center, wrapped in white.

Cap the extra space at roughly 60% of the ad's own area. Strong advises 20% additional whitespace gives the greatest cost-adjusted gain, and above 60% attention value doesn't compensate the added cost.
Compare against benchmarks: Poffenberger/Strong found a white-wrapped half-page scored 176% attention vs. 141% for a standard full-page and 100% for a plain half-page.

Use the same principle in digital layout: increase hero whitespace around a single core message module rather than cramming more elements into the same space; keep number of visual elements to a minimum.
Combine with the checklist preference for sufficient whitespace and a single obvious focus point.
caveats: The 60% and 20% thresholds are from Strong's print-era guidance; test in digital.
Whitespace helps ad attention but doesn't substitute for a strong offer and clear headline.

cards.title: Guarantee Credibility with Concrete Facts, Examples, and Specificity
cards.summary: Replace vague statistics with vivid examples and extreme specifics to build believability and make claims more persuasive.
cards.use_when: Writing PDP copy, testimonial sections, pitch decks for offer pages, and any proof blocks in ads or landing pages.
steps: Convert abstract stats into concrete examples and stories where possible; the source's point is that audiences trust specific narratives over round numbers.
Apply extreme specificity throughout: 'Powerful Web Pages Designed in 24 Hours by Famous Marketing Expert for $199' communicates more than 'Get a great website fast.'
Put a specific proof element in the headline itself—time-to-deliver, expertise, exact price—to qualify attention from the right prospects.
Pair claims with testimonials. The checklist treats testimonials as mandatory if you have none; get them.

Use 6-shot persuasion logic from the Influence Cues: the source's weapons include reciprocation, commitment, social proof, liking, authority, and scarcity—sprinkle each in your proof blocks where honest.
caveats: The 25% headline-quotes reading boost is a source-cited figure; treat as directional.
Specificity must remain truthful; the source emphasizes believable copy and not overblown claims.

cards.title: Convert Feature Specs into Bottom-Line Benefits
cards.summary: Move past features into the single core benefit—the bottom-line outcome—and build copy around it in a logical Get-Attention → Interest → Desire → Proof → Action progression.
cards.use_when: Rewriting PDP descriptions, ad copy, and email body copy where the text is heavy with specs but light on why the customer should care.
steps: Identify one core benefit (the bottom-line reader payoff, not the feature) and center the ad or PDP around it. The #1 checklist rule: headline must feature the product's biggest benefit.
Map the means-end chain from attribute → consequence → bottom-line value for the buyer, and write the ad at the end of that chain.
Progress the copy logically: grab attention, stimulate interest, build desire, offer proof, then ask for action.
Load the body with benefits—not bragging about your company—and put 'you' in the first few words of the first sentence.
Sell one product per ad. Catalog-style exceptions exist for delis and furniture stores that show 'everything we got,' but for most products one is best.
Close with a specific action request: 'clip this coupon,' 'bring it by August 21,' or for ecommerce a clear 'Add to cart' plus deadline if genuine.
caveats: Very long catalog-style lists work in specific categories; don't impose single-product rule universally.
Benefits must stay believable; overblown claims cost credibility per the checklist.

cards.title: Wrap Copy With Short Sentences, Simple Words, and Serif/Sans Choice
cards.summary: Readability lifts response: short sentences, common words, thick paragraph breaks, personal pronouns, and matching typeface to medium (serif for print, sans-serif for web).
cards.use_when: Editing product descriptions, landing-page body copy, and email copy for readability and per-word impact.
steps: Write short sentences and simple, common words; cut fluff. Use the Flesch Reading Ease Score if you want a numeric check.
Keep paragraphs short and indent them to make the page easier to scan in print; online, use 1–2 sentence blocks or bulleted benefit lists instead.
Favor 'you,' 'your,' 'you're' over 'we/our.' The checklist asks if 'you' appears in the first few words of the opening sentence.
Set typeface by medium: serif typefaces (such as Schoolbook) for print; sans-serif (Arial, Verdana) for web. Limit type styles to one or two, three maximum.
Break long copy with selling subheads and captions under photos so skimmers still absorb benefit points.
Use powerful visual adjectives where appropriate to direct mental movies, but keep modifiers that carry meaning—cut the rest.
caveats: Flesch's score is a rough guide; product complexity may require longer sentences without loss.
Typestyles recommendations come from print-era practice; modern web systems vary, verify current best practice for your platform.

cards.title: Build the Killer Ad Checklist Before Launch
cards.summary: Use the 46-point killer ad checklist as a pre-launch gate to ensure headline, body, layout, and proof elements are in place before spending on any ad.
cards.use_when: Reviewing any ad, PDP hero, or campaign creative just before publishing; a sanity gate to catch missing headline, proof, or CTA elements.
steps: Headline: confirm it features the product's biggest benefit, is a real grabber with emotional pull, is much larger than body copy, uses initial caps (ALL CAPS only if 4-5 words), and makes an offer.
Body first sentence: uses a jump-starter, flows naturally from the headline, gets into benefits immediately, and puts 'you' early.
Body general: focus on reader benefit, why buy from you versus alternatives, emotions, specificity, short paragraphs, and the logical AIDA-style progression ending in a super-simple action ask.
Proof and close: include testimonials, a deadline where appropriate, bulleted benefits if there are many, a keyed response mechanism for attribution, and a large phone/contact identifier plus logo.

Layout: professional designer, big bold headline broken at the right words, one clear focus, sufficient white space (consider white-wrap), indented paragraphs, minimum typestyles, relevant art, and a person looking at the reader where appropriate.
caveats: Treat as a checklist, not a scoring rubric—more ingredients correlate with success in the source's experience but do not guarantee it.
Not all items apply to every format (e.g., coupon items don't apply to a short display ad).

cards.title: Make Buying Ridiculously Easy, Every Step
cards.summary: Remove friction across the whole purchase path—channels, payment methods, guarantees, and installments—because ease is a measurable response lever.
cards.use_when: Auditing cart and checkout flow, payment options, contact methods, and order completion steps on an ecommerce store.
steps: List all accepted order channels: phone, mail, online, fax (context-dependent), plus credit cards and personal checks. Get a toll-free number where market-appropriate.
For higher-priced items, offer installment payments. The source cites '3 easy payments of just $10.99' for products over $15 as boosting response 15 percent.
Offer a long strong guarantee longer than your competition's, an explicit statement 'It's easy to order...', and clear contact info (street, email, web address, phone).
For physical stores and hybrid, include directions, parking advice, maps, or landmarks—those are more necessary than you may think.
Use a Bill Me or credit option; the source cites this as lifting response 50 percent or more in direct mail contexts. Adapt as a pay-later or installment checkout option for ecommerce.
Tell the reader exactly what to do in super-simple terms: clip, click, bring by date, save amount.
caveats: 50%+ Bill Me lift and 15% installment lift are direct-mail figures; treat as directional in ecommerce and validate with your own test.
Fax/mail ordering is legacy; port the principle—more accepted channels and less friction—rather than the literal steps.

cards.title: Boost Coupon/Offer Returns With 11 Tactics
cards.summary: Eleven coupon-design tactics, from headline instruction to check-off boxes and arrows, to lift redemption of discounts and promos.
cards.use_when: Designing discount codes, promo banners, cart coupons, or insert coupons to maximize click and redemption.
steps: Instruct the reader in the headline or subhead to return the coupon; say 'Buy 1 Get 1 Free!' instead of '50% Off' where applicable.
Place a big 'FREE!' at the top of the ad and tell what the coupon brings inside the coupon itself—say it again.
Show what the coupon brings via a small photo or illustration so the value is visible.
Use a bold coupon border, say 'Valuable Coupon' at the top, and point to it with bold arrows.
Set a hard deadline (firm date) or soft deadline ('The first 100 people...') to break buyer inertia.
Provide check-off boxes to get involvement—for ecommerce, port this as selectable bundle options or a configured offer.
Give sufficient room for fill-ins (or, in digital, ample tap targets and clear form fields).
caveats: Coupon mechanics from direct mail may translate imperfectly to email or in-app offers; test formats.
Forced scarcity language ('first 100') must be true to avoid credibility damage.

cards.title: Use Fear, Identity, and Social Proof Ethically in Ad Copy
cards.summary: Multiple persuasion levers—fear, ego morphing, bandwagon, social proof, authority, commitment—can be layered into ads, each with a specific mechanism and risk.
cards.use_when: Choosing which persuasion angle to lead with in a paid ad campaign or landing page (e.g., fear-based for problem categories, identity-based for aspirational products).
steps: For problems the buyer already recognizes, induce fear based on existing fears rather than inventing new ones (like Listerine's bad-breath play). Escalate with stress-causing copy that names consequences of inaction.

Use ego morphing / instant identification for products tied to aspirational groups (e.g., Abercrombie & Fitch). Show the buyer the version of themselves they want—the source calls this 'Life-Force 8' territory of survival and sex.
Apply social proof and bandwagon: show that similar buyers already chose you, and make the group visible.
Lean on authority positioning—expert credentials, endorsements, third-party seals (e.g., Good Housekeeping Seal) —for categories where skepticism is high.
Leverage commitment and consistency: small yes steps (a free starter kit, a quiz) make the larger purchase easier.
Time the message with the transtheoretical stages (precontemplation, contemplation, preparation, action, maintenance) so your angle matches where the buyer is.
caveats: Fear appeals can cause avoidance or brand dislike if the threat is overblown or the solution feels unattainable.
The 6 weapons of influence are drawn from Cialdini's Influence; high-pressure tactics carry reputational risk in ecommerce where reviews are public.

cards.title: Match Message to Peripheral or Central Processing Audience
cards.summary: The Elaboration Likelihood Model says superficial thinkers respond to peripheral cues (visuals, authority, likability) while engaged buyers respond to central cues (evidence, arguments).
cards.use_when: Deciding whether an ad or PDP should lead with emotional/visual cues versus deep evidence, based on how motivated the target audience is.
steps: For low-involvement purchases or impulse categories, lead with peripheral cues: strong visuals, celebrity or expert endorsement, likability, repetition, and simple heuristics (rules of thumb).
For high-involvement, considered purchases, lead with central route content: detailed benefits, evidence, comparisons, and demonstrations to build durable attitude change.
For long copy that must serve both, front-load peripheral grabs (headline, image of a person looking at the reader, authority) and then deliver the central proof later.
Use visual adjectives, action photos, and mental-movie direction for peripheral audiences; factual proof and testimonials for central ones.
Recognize that an ecommerce shopper can shift processing mode during the session—landing-page curiosity may not carry into the checkout where proof matters.
caveats: The ELM is a theoretical model; the source only sketches it—apply with judgment, not as a fixed formula.
Superficial/peripheral audiences still buy; do not infer that low-involvement means low-quality content.

cards.title: Test Offers, Headlines, and Message Sideness Before Scaling
cards.summary: Systematically test offers and ad components; frame messages with the right sidedness (one-sided vs. acknowledging counter-arguments) and use surveys before assuming you know the audience.
cards.use_when: Structuring A/B tests for PDPs, ad creatives, or offer variants before scaling spend; also for post-purchase surveys and review-based research.
steps: Treat offers as the primary test variable—the source's secret #33 emphasizes guarantees but the same logic applies to bundle structure, urgency, and price framing.
Test headline variations including the headline-starter frameworks (22 psychological starters) and one with a guarantee or deadline.

Consider message sidedness: for audiences already favorable or low-involvement, a one-sided message works; where skepticism or counter-arguments are strong, acknowledge and refute them (Inoculation Theory: warn and defend).
Use survey power: ask existing customers and prospects what they believe, fear, and want, before writing claims.
Track keyed response sources so you can attribute results per creative, per channel, per offer.
Run a single change at a time where possible to isolate the driver; combine with the killer checklist to ensure each variant is fully composed.
caveats: Small sample tests can produce false signals; account for seasonality and traffic mix.
The Inoculation Theory framing (warning of attacks, refuting them) may backfire if the attack is unknown to the audience—don't invent controversy.

cards.title: Run Deadline-Driven Urgency Without Cheating the Buyer
cards.summary: Deadlines, limited offers, and scarcity cues break inertia; use them honestly and match them to the buyer's stage.
cards.use_when: Designing cart-abandon, flash-sale, or limited-stock promo copy where urgency is the lever being applied.
steps: Use hard deadlines (specific date) for genuine time limits and soft deadlines ('First 100 people...') where supply is truly limited.
Frame one-day sales as one-day sales; the source's 'one-day sales' and 'while supplies last' phrases are basic tension-reducing urgency lines that have proven durable.
Set a deadline in routine ad copy most of the time (per checklist: 'Most of the time it is!').
Combine scarcity with the guarantee to reduce downside risk—buyers respond to limited time when the risk of buying is also low.
For ecommerce, apply to flash drops, restocks, and seasonal edits—so the scarcity is real (stock counts, real end times) and doesn't become 'always-on' urgency, which erodes trust.
caveats: Fake scarcity diminishes credibility and can breach consumer-protection rules in some jurisdictions; the source's examples presume honest limits.
Urgency works differently for considered purchases; it may rush buyers into regret and returns.

cards.title: Use Testimonials, Photos, Captions, and Person-Looking Photos for Proof
cards.summary: Specific visual and proof conventions—real testimonials, action photos, captions, and a person's gaze—lift ad performance and reduce reader skepticism.
cards.use_when: Optimizing PDP images, testimonial sections, ad creative, and any place where visual proof supports conversion.
steps: Always include testimonials—if you don't have them, collect them. Position them near the point of decision on the PDP.
Show what you're selling; action shots are best. Pair with selling captions, because captions are read more than body copy.

Choose from the source's seven best photo types, including a person looking directly at the reader (one of the most powerful attention-grabbers) and art relevant to the sales message (no babies for steel-belted tire ads).
Use demonstrations and pseudo-movement (implied motion from the image) to convey function; demonstration is a core credibility signal.
Avoid reverse-type pitfalls; limited types styles (one or two, three max); sufficient whitespace and a single clear focus; indented paragraphs (print) or short scannable blocks (web).
Add authority visual cues—credential badges, signature on guarantee, certifications—to pair with written proof.
caveats: The 7-photo-types list and reverse-type pitfall percentages are generalized; specific optimal imagery varies by category and platform.
Person-looking photos can increase attention but may compete with the CTA if placed poorly—place with intent.

cards.title: Match Long Copy or Short Copy to the Buying Situation
cards.summary: Long copy works when the reader is engaged and the offer merits detail; short copy wins when the reader needs only a quick reason to act—test rather than assume.
cards.use_when: Choosing ad format or PDP body length for a specific category (e.g., impulse product vs. considered high-ticket purchase).
steps: Assess reader motivation: for complex, higher-priced, or unfamiliar products, long, benefit-stacked copy performs well because engaged buyers want more reasons and proof.
For low-involvement, low-price, impulse categories, short copy is often best—get to the point and to the CTA quickly.
Break long copy with subheads, bullets, and captions so skimmers still get the argument; do not write long copy without wayfinding.
Use the AIDA structure in long copy (attention, interest, desire, proof, action) so length serves a purpose rather than padding.
Run a controlled test of long versus short variants and compare purchase conversion (not just time on page or CTR).
caveats: No universal rule: the source explicitly frames long/short as situational; treat it as an experimental choice.
Platform constraints (e.g., character-limited social ads) may dictate length regardless of reader motivation.

cards.title: Give Yourself a 'Cleverectomy' When Creative Argues With Performance
cards.summary: Reject creative for creative's sake; advertising is business communication whose purpose is to sell, and copy that impresses friends but not prospects wastes spend.
cards.use_when: Resolving disagreements between design/creative stakeholders and performance marketers over ad or PDP creative direction.
steps: Set the goal at the outset: advertising exists to sell, not to win awards or entertain. Use Rosser Reeves's framing—when sales are falling, you want the curve to turn, not fine writing.
Ask the headline to pass the 'so what is being sold?' test. If the reader can't tell from the headline alone, rewrite it.
Redirect the argument away from cleverness toward the specifics that sell: benefits, facts, an offer, reassurance. Note that 'interesting' doesn't equal 'clever.'
Engage in test-based resolution rather than taste debates: if the team loves a clever concept, run it against a direct one and compare sales-based outcomes.
Use the practical example: 'Powerful Web Pages Designed in 24 Hours by Famous Marketing Expert for $199' beats 'Sticky Web' because it communicates the product, time, credibility, and price.
caveats: The source's strong 'creative is wasted' position is opinionated; brand-building campaigns sometimes prioritize memorability and recall over immediate response.
Pure direct-response testing tools may not capture long-run brand effects; use both metrics where viable.
